segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On Tuesday Mrs Pike came into the vestry with the banns already settled in her own mind, and found Mr Rowe writing up a burial.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: Three Sundays, beginning with the next. Miss Selby and Mr Dene. You need not trouble yourself over the particulars, for I have them all, and her father was a clergyman in Berkshire.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mr Rowe put down the pen.

segments.speaker: Mr Silas Rowe
segments.text: I am sure you have them, ma'am. I shall read banns when Mr Dene and Miss Selby come to me and ask me for them. That is the whole of my practice and I have never varied it.

segments.speaker: Mr Silas Rowe
segments.text: Then they may be shy of me in this room, and I shall be very glad of it. I do not publish a marriage at the word of a third person, however kindly the word is meant.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said it with perfect civility, and Mrs Pike went down the path observing to herself that eighty pounds a year had never made a man so grand before.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
By Thursday Mrs Pike had the week arranged for them. There was the walk to Nine Acres on Wednesday, and boiled fowl at her own table on Thursday, and Margaret was to take Mr Dene's arm along the church path on Sunday where the whole green could see it done.

On the Nine Acres road Dene talked about the Ludd boy, who could do long division in his head and could not be got to hold a pen above a minute together. Margaret found she had asked three questions, and had wanted the answers to all three. At the piano afterwards he turned her page a bar early, and apologised, and turned the next one early too.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On Friday she came up to the schoolroom with the singing book under her arm. The window was propped open with a slate, and Dene was inside with the schoolmaster from Bramdean, who had walked over about a globe.

segments.speaker: Mr Robert Dene
segments.text: The moment her aunt is on the coach I shall put an end to it. It has gone a great deal further than I ever meant it to go, and I have no business in it at all. A man on forty pounds a year has no business in it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
Margaret stood on the gravel with the book against her and did not go in. She laid it on the sill instead, where he would find it.

He came out at the sound and caught her at the gate.

segments.speaker: Mr Robert Dene
segments.text: You are early. Will you come in and hear them? They have the round in three parts now, after a fashion.

segments.speaker: Miss Margaret Selby
segments.text: Thank you, no. I shall be ready at four, as Mrs Pike arranged.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Her hands were folded. Dene had learnt in a fortnight what that meant, and had not yet learnt what to do about it.

segments.speaker: Mr Robert Dene
segments.text: Miss Selby. Have I said something?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Mrs Pike was already coming up the lane with Mrs Ferris beside her, the two of them walking at the pace of women who mean to arrive before anything is finished. Margaret turned and wished them both good morning. Mrs Ferris looked at her niece over the top of her spectacles, and then rather longer at Mr Dene.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: Nerves. It is always nerves, so near the banns.

segments.speaker: Mrs Augusta Ferris
segments.text: I have seen a good many engaged couples, ma'am. That is not nerves. That is a young woman who has heard something she was not meant to hear, and I should very much like to know what it was.
